Beckham was one of the few Democrats to vote against the repeal of Prohibition, a position he held until his death in 1922.

Beckham had an extensive career in public service, serving as mayor of New York City from 1894 to 1896, lieutenant governor of New York from 1897 to 1900, United States senator from 1900 to 1903, and vice president of the United States from 1903 to 1909. During his presidency, he signed the Morrill Land Grant Act of 1887, which provided $1.5 million to build a railroad from Yellowstone National Park in Montana to the Yukon-Kuskokwim Delta in Alaska. The railroad was completed in 1891 and named for President Grover Cleveland, who had helped fund its construction.

In the early 1900s, Beckham began a campaign to bring the Panama Canal to New York and, after winning the Democratic nomination for governor in 1904, he became the first governor in the nation to use the power of eminent domain to acquire land for the canal. The land was purchased at a cost of $10 million, with Beckham's name on the deed as co-beneficiary. In 1906, a group of investors led by George Pullman of Pullman-Standard attempted to take control of the canal by filing a lawsuit

After the Napoleonic Wars the British Army took over the defence of Australia, with the exception of the Northern Territory, which was in the hands of the Native Australian tribes. During the Boer War (1899-1902) the Australian Expeditionary Force (AEF) was formed to fight the South African War in the Kimberley and Cape Flaccos. In World War I (1914-1918) the AEF played a major role in the Gallipoli campaign against the Ottomans and fought in North Africa, the Middle East and the Balkan Peninsula. After the Armistice in 1918 there was a period of peace and then the First World War broke out in Europe. Australia was at war with Germany and Austria-Hungary, and in November 1918 the AEF was re-organised into the Territorial Army of the Australian Expeditionary Force (TAF). This was an amalgamation of the Australian Army, Naval Service and Auxiliary Air Force, and its purpose was to provide a reserve force for the war effort.

. This paper is the first to use these data to examine the evolution of a group of early tetrapod taxa that had been neglected until then.

The authors show that, contrary to expectations based on the hypothesis of monophyly of the group, there is no evidence for a "Tetrapod Trilemma" that is supported by all of the data. Instead, the data are consistent with an evolutionary history in which temnospondyls diverged from all other tetrapods at different times and in different lineages. This is in contrast to the view that temnospondyls are sister to all other tetrapods, and that their divergence dates back to the origin of vertebrates. In addition, the authors present a new cladistic analysis that is consistent with the idea that temnospondyls are the most derived members of the group.

Adam Yates is a postdoctoral researcher at the University of California, Berkeley. Anne Warren is an assistant professor of geosciences at Oregon State University. Their paper is published in the open access journal PeerJ. (DOI: 10.7717/peerj.3159)

Synopsis Edit

The Eleventh Doctor and Clara travel to an old school for a field trip, but things go awry when they are mistaken for schoolchildren. The school is run by a man called Mr Troughton, who has taken a liking to Clara after seeing her in the news. However, Clara is in a bit of a pickle, as Troughton's assistant, the Headmistress, wants her to stay at the school for her own safety and that of the school's students.

Clara finds herself in a race against time to escape her pursuers, and it's up to her to decide what she should do with the TARDIS key that is given to her by the Doctor. Meanwhile, the Doctor's friends and enemies begin to make their presence known in the school, and they have no intention of letting Clara go unscathed.

A new study by University of California, San Diego archaeologist Michael Coe provides the first evidence that the Olmec were involved in the domestication of maize (corn), the world's most important food crop. This is significant because it shows that they had a long-term commitment to agricultural development and may have played a role in the spread of maize to Mesoamerica, the New World and South America.

Coe, a postdoctoral researcher in the department of anthropology at UC San Diego, analyzed pollen and stone tools from archaeological sites in the Olmec heartland and compared them to maize domestication in the region. His findings, published in the May issue of the peer-reviewed journal PLOS ONE, show that the Olmec were the first to domesticate maize, which was introduced to the region by the Mayans and Aztecs about 2,000 years ago.

Tinsley-Wyndham's design for the memorial was based on a sketch he had made of the gate in 1864, and included an obelisk at the top of the gate, flanked by a pair of lions and a man in a chariot pulling a wheelbarrow. The lion was supposed to symbolise the Union of the Crowns, and the chariot was a reference to the loss of the Kings and Queens of England in the Napoleonic Wars. In addition, there was a bronze statue of Queen Victoria on horseback, which was placed in front of the obelisk.

The gate was built of granite, and it took three years to complete. The memorial was dedicated at a ceremony in St Paul's Cathedral on 24 July 1864, attended by the Duke of Wellington, Lord Salisbury, Prince Albert of Saxe-Coburg and Gotha, and other dignitaries.
